fullTitle: Burning and Suppression of Solids
statusBasis: NASA's Combustion Science page lists BASS among archived experiments; PSI record gives a closed investigation period.

hardware.apparatus: Small flow duct (76 mm × 76 mm cross-section), variable-speed fan, 29-gauge Kanthal wire igniter
hardware.notes: The PSI record describes fabric samples and other shapes (spheres, cylinders) burned in opposed or concurrent airflow.

sources.title: Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)

fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Fabric sheets in a 76 mm × 76 mm duct; additional sphere and cylinder samples
fuelSpecs.notes: Material list and geometry come from the PSI record's approach summary.

suppressantsTested: Gaseous nitrogen (inert extinguishing agent, per PSI record)
testConditions.notes: PSI documents airflow up to 40 cm/s, opposed or concurrent. It does not state pressure or oxygen setpoints; those remain Unknown in this dataset rather than being assumed from ISS cabin conditions.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Bridge the gap between the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 screening method and actual microgravity material flammability, and assess an inert gaseous extinguishing agent across materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
variedParameters: Airflow speed and direction (opposed vs concurrent)
sensorsAndDiagnostics: Top and edge-view cameras for flame size, shape, color and spread rate
Glovebox instrumentation for flow and environment (as described in PSI record)
experimentalDesign.notes: The PSI record summarises the design but does not list every sensor or a complete test matrix.

findings: BASS flame behavior was highly sensitive to forced-flow changes in the 0–5 cm/s range. In some tests, flames persisted below 1 cm/s as dim, blue, comparatively stable flames; a sudden increase in airflow could make them flare up.

For acrylic slab samples, even the smallest observed flames burned for more than five minutes before self-extinguishing. This is a result for the tested samples/configurations, not a general duration for spacecraft fires.
Fuel preheating and moderate flow (about 1–5 cm/s) increased solid temperature and vaporization, strengthening and brightening the flame over time.
findingsNote: These findings are from specific BASS test configurations reported in NASA publications. They do not establish universal fire behavior or a safe operating limit for spacecraft materials.
modelingUtility: The PSI record states that BASS results are used in first-order models of heat release in spacecraft fires and to extend cone-calorimeter data toward performance-based material selection.
terrestrialApplications: Improved understanding of opposed- and concurrent-flow flame spread relevant to fires in confined spaces (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Direct solid-fuel flammability and suppression data in the ISS glovebox; strong spacecraft relevance, with no quantitative findings in the PSI summary.

fullTitle: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
status: Completed — archived NASA investigation; summary report published 2021
statusBasis: NASA/TM-20210011385 is the BASS-II summary report (October 2021), and the PSI record gives a closed investigation period. BASS-II is treated as completed on that basis.

hardware.apparatus: Small wind tunnel inside MSG with variable-speed fan; opposed and concurrent flow; 29-gauge Kanthal igniter
hardware.notes: BASS-II reused and extended the BASS flow-duct approach in the MSG.

materials: Other solid samples across PI test matrices
fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Rods, spherical sections, slabs, films and fabric sheets; sample thicknesses in the PI matrices range from about 0.1 mm to several mm
fuelSpecs.notes: Material and geometry lists are taken from the PSI record and NASA/TM-20210011385 test matrices.

suppressantsTested: Gaseous nitrogen (diluent used to lower oxygen concentration; the PSI summary does not characterize it as a suppression agent)
testConditions.notes: NASA/TM-20210011385 reports ambient O2 varied from 21% down to 16% and a 1 atm test condition, with duct flows from 0 to 55 cm/s in some configurations. The PSI record instead says airflow up to 40 cm/s. The discrepancy is preserved; both are cited.

sources.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II (BASS–II) Summary Report

experimentalDesign.objectives: Study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flow; bridge 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 screening and microgravity flammability; provide preliminary data for SoFIE science requirements.
variedParameters: Ambient oxygen concentration via nitrogen dilution
Sample geometry (rods, spherical sections, slabs, films, fabrics)
sensorsAndDiagnostics: Oxygen and carbon-dioxide sensors (CSA-CP and CDM readings reported separately)
Radiometers and thermocouples in PI configurations
Post-test sample mass loss and imagery
experimentalDesign.notes: Diagnostics varied by PI sub-experiment; see NASA/TM-20210011385.

findings: Oxygen was consumed nearly stoichiometrically to CO2, and measured CO/CO2 ratios were about an order of magnitude higher than in efficient flue gases, indicating inefficient flames.
Heat release estimated by oxygen-consumption calorimetry was mostly well below 100 W; the one test approaching 100 W damaged a window corner after a leak directed heat there.
The global equivalence ratio averaged about 1.3, indicating fuel-rich burning under low-velocity forced flow.
Crew observations and flow sweeps outlined a U-shaped flammability boundary, including blowoff extinction at high flow and quenching-type extinction at low flow.
BASS-II tests were especially flow-sensitive between 0 and 5 cm/s. Some flames could persist below 1 cm/s in a dim-blue state and flare when flow increased.
findingsNote: The BASS-II summary and earlier BASS-II presentation use slightly different maximum duct-flow values (up to 55 cm/s in the report and 53 cm/s in the presentation). See the cited source-specific conditions; do not treat this dataset as the complete raw run log.
modelingUtility: Provides benchmark solid-fuel flame-spread data and a U-shaped flammability boundary used to validate microgravity flame-spread and material-screening models.
terrestrialApplications: Fire-spread and flammability modeling relevant to terrestrial fires and material screening (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Combines solid-fuel flammability, suppression-relevant extinction limits, a documented test matrix and a published summary report with quantitative results.

fullTitle: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I
investigationPeriod: Flight test: 2016-06-14; PSI-98 project metadata lists 2001-03-02 to 2008-02-28 (conflict)
status: Completed — large-scale test on an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle after departure
statusBasis: NASA records conflict: the PSI-98 page lists project dates from 2001–2008 and a mismatched proposal title, while NASA mission material dates Saffire-I operations to June 14, 2016. The older dates are retained only as repository metadata, not as the flight date.

hardware.apparatus: Large flow duct with fan-driven flow, flow straighteners, two cameras, thermocouples, two radiometers, O2/CO2 sensors and two anemometers
hardware.notes: Saffire flew on an expendable cargo vehicle so a large fire could be studied without crew risk.

materials: SIBAL composite fabric: 75% cotton on a 25% fiberglass substrate by weight
fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Approximately 0.94 m long × 0.4 m wide sample card

testConditions.notes: NASA results report an initial ISS oxygen reading of 21.7%; this was an observed vehicle atmosphere reading, not a deliberately prescribed setpoint. The result paper reports 20 cm/s duct flow. Pressure and local O2 time series should be taken from the raw record.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and compare low-g flammability limits with NASA's normal-gravity material screening test.
variedParameters: Airflow direction (per record: concurrent or opposed)
sensorsAndDiagnostics: Thermocouples for flow, flame and plume temperature
Solid-state pressure, CO2 and O2 sensors

findings: NASA reports a 40.6 × 94 cm SIBAL sample and 20 cm/s forced flow. The initial ISS oxygen reading was 21.7%.

The concurrent-flow test ran for 420 s and reached about 84 cm of spread along the 94 cm sample (about 1.8 mm/s). The opposed-flow contingency test lasted 70 s and spread about 10 cm (about 1.3 mm/s).

The concurrent flame reached a constrained size after ignition, unlike the accelerating upward spread typically observed in 1-g tests. NASA also reports that enclosure/duct scale affected spread, so small-duct results should not be transferred directly to a spacecraft-sized geometry.
findingsNote: The PSI-98 page itself has a date/proposal metadata conflict. Flight results here are sourced to NASA mission material and the NASA results report. The 84 cm value is measured spread length, not burned fuel mass.
modelingUtility: Provides large-scale, realistic spacecraft-fire data intended to validate material-selection criteria and fire-growth models.
terrestrialApplications: Fire safety in sealed environments such as mines, aircraft and submarines (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Rare large-scale microgravity fire data directly relevant to spacecraft material screening and fire-growth assumptions.

fullTitle: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II
investigationPeriod: Flight tests: 2016-11-21; PSI project period: 2016-09-30 to 2017-04-01
status: Completed — multi-sample large-scale test on Cygnus
statusBasis: PSI record describes the flight on the Cygnus resupply vehicle and a closed investigation period.

hardware.apparatus: Saffire flow duct with a sample card holding 9 samples; two cameras, thermocouples, radiometers, O2/CO2 and pressure sensors, two anemometers

fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: 9 samples, each 5 cm × 29 cm, on one sample card

testConditions.notes: NASA results report 20 cm/s for samples 2-1 to 2-5 and 2-7 to 2-9, and 25 cm/s for sample 2-6. Initial ISS O2 reading was approximately 22.1%; distinguish this ambient reading from a controlled oxygen sweep. Most tests were concurrent-flow; sample 2-4 was opposed-flow.

namedConditions.label: Sample 2-1 · silicone, 0.27 mm
namedConditions.note: Concurrent; insignificant spread; ~0 mm microgravity burn length.

namedConditions.label: Sample 2-2 · silicone, 0.61 mm
namedConditions.note: Concurrent; insignificant spread; ~0 mm microgravity burn length.

namedConditions.label: Sample 2-3 · silicone, 1.03 mm
namedConditions.note: Concurrent; insignificant spread; ~0 mm microgravity burn length.

namedConditions.label: Sample 2-4 · silicone, 0.37 mm
namedConditions.note: Opposed-flow; insignificant spread; ~0 mm microgravity burn length.

namedConditions.label: Sample 2-5 · SIBAL fabric
namedConditions.note: Concurrent; 145 s burn duration; 29 cm spread; 2.1 mm/s.

namedConditions.label: Sample 2-6 · SIBAL fabric
namedConditions.note: Concurrent; 115 s burn duration; 29 cm spread; 2.6 mm/s.

namedConditions.label: Sample 2-7 · PMMA lead-in + Nomex
namedConditions.note: Concurrent; PMMA portion consumed but Nomex did not ignite.

namedConditions.label: Sample 2-8 · grooved PMMA slab
namedConditions.note: 600 s; ~10 cm visibly damaged; flame anchored near the sample base.

namedConditions.label: Sample 2-9 · flat PMMA slab
namedConditions.note: 900 s; ~10 cm visibly damaged; flame anchored near the sample base.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Determine large-fire growth rate in low gravity and compare low-g flammability limits with NASA's normal-gravity screening test.

findings: Saffire-II tested nine 5 × 29 cm samples in an uncrewed Cygnus vehicle. Initial ISS oxygen was about 22.1%; duct flow was 20 cm/s except sample 2-6 at 25 cm/s. The campaign compared silicone, SIBAL fabric, a PMMA/Nomex composite, and grooved and flat PMMA.

The 0.27–1.03 mm silicone samples showed insignificant microgravity spread under these tests. The two SIBAL samples each spread the 29 cm sample length: 2.1 mm/s at 20 cm/s flow and 2.6 mm/s at 25 cm/s flow.

In the PMMA/Nomex composite, the PMMA lead-in burned but the Nomex did not ignite. The two 1 cm PMMA slab tests lasted 600 s and 900 s, with about 10 cm of visibly damaged material; the flames stayed anchored near the sample base and regressed slowly (reported as 0.01–0.04 mm/s).
These results are material- and configuration-specific. They do not establish a single spacecraft-wide oxygen flammability limit.
findingsNote: Values summarize NASA Table I and its footnotes. The approximately 22.1% value is the initial ISS oxygen reading; it was not a broad controlled oxygen sweep. “Insignificant spread” is NASA’s qualitative description, not a zero-uncertainty numerical measurement.
modelingUtility: Extends Saffire-I to multiple materials and provides data for validating flame-spread and material-screening models.
terrestrialApplications: Fire behaviour in confined, sealed environments (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Multi-material large-scale fire test relevant to spacecraft material selection; numerical findings are not in the PSI summary.

investigationPeriod: Flight test: 2017-06-04; PSI project record begins 2017-04-18 and omits an end date
status: Completed — large-scale test at higher forced flow
statusBasis: NASA reports Saffire-III operations in June 2017. A NASA development/planning paper lists 30 cm/s, while the later NASA results presentation and results table report the flown tests at 25 cm/s; the detail page uses the executed value and preserves the planning discrepancy.

hardware.facility: Cygnus cargo vehicle (PSI record lists ISS as flight platform)
hardware.apparatus: Saffire flow duct with camera, thermocouple, radiometer, O2/CO2, pressure and anemometry instrumentation

fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Not stated in PSI record
fuelSpecs.notes: Material is stated; sample dimensions are not.

testConditions.notes: Executed-flow sources report 25 cm/s for Saffire-III. An earlier NASA planning paper lists 30 cm/s; that appears to be a planned rather than executed value. Initial oxygen reading was about 21.2%, not a controlled O2 sweep.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Determine large-fire growth rate in low gravity and compare low-g flammability limits with NASA's normal-gravity screening test.

findings: Saffire-III used the same 40.6 × 94 cm SIBAL fabric sample as Saffire-I. NASA’s results summary reports 25 cm/s executed airflow (an earlier planning document listed 30 cm/s) and an initial oxygen reading near 21.2%.
The concurrent-flow test spread about 84 cm in 300 s (about 2.3 mm/s); the opposed-flow test spread about 10 cm in 60 s (about 0.98 mm/s).
The results show that spread rate changed with flow direction and speed in these tested configurations; they are not a general scaling law for all materials or spacecraft airflow fields.

modelingUtility: Provides large-scale fire-spread data at an executed flow of 25 cm/s, compared with Saffire-I at 20 cm/s, for evaluating flow effects in the tested configuration.
terrestrialApplications: Fire safety in sealed environments (PSI record, stated for the Saffire series)

relevanceScores.rationale: Large-scale fire test at a higher flow than Saffire-I; useful for flow-effect comparisons, but no results in the PSI summary.

fullTitle: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
status: Completed — smoke-particle measurement in the MSG
statusBasis: PSI record describes on-orbit operations in the Microgravity Science Glovebox and lists a closed investigation period.

hardware.apparatus: Near-field smoke source hardware, Far Field Box, two smoke detectors, thermophoretic soot samplers, video cameras

materials: Overheated spacecraft materials (specific materials listed in SAME-R record and publications)
fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Small heated samples; geometry not stated in the SAME PSI summary
fuelSpecs.notes: The PSI summary says smoke was generated by overheated spacecraft materials with controlled sample temperature, flow field and particle aging time.

testConditions.notes: No oxygen, pressure or airflow values are stated in the PSI summary. The experiment ran in ISS cabin conditions inside the MSG, but cabin values are not asserted as test parameters here.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Quantify liquid smoke particle sizes produced in low gravity and relate the droplet size distribution to smoke generation and transport conditions.
sensorsAndDiagnostics: Two smoke detectors (response recorded on video)
Thermophoretic soot samplers analysed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
experimentalDesign.notes: Combustion events typically lasted about 2 minutes; igniter operated for 15–60 s.

findings: SAME measured smoke aerosols from spacecraft materials including Kapton and Teflon. The NASA summary reports particles below 300 nm and a low-gravity count-mean diameter typically about 50% larger than under comparable normal-gravity conditions.

The particle-size result suggested sub-micrometer measurement could help distinguish smoke from spacecraft dust, but it was a research implication rather than a validated operational detector threshold.
NASA smoke-transport modeling predicted that detection time can be long and strongly dependent on detector location and cabin geometry that blocks or redirects ventilation.
findingsNote: Particle size and transport depend on material, heating, airflow, and detector location. The reported comparison is not a universal size multiplier for every spacecraft fire.
modelingUtility: Supports development of smoke-particle growth models and reduced-gravity smoke-detector performance evaluation.
terrestrialApplications: Smoke detection in submarines and underwater laboratories (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Core detection-focused investigation with direct smoke-detector hardware relevance; PSI summary lacks measured outcomes.

fullTitle: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight
statusBasis: PSI record states flight tests ran from 16 July to 9 September 2010 and completed 66 test points.

hardware.apparatus: SAME hardware with an added in-house M-pass instrument replacing one Commercial Diagnostic Enclosure

materials: Other spacecraft materials listed in PSI keywords
fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Not stated in PSI summary
fuelSpecs.notes: SAME-R replaced the original DBP samples with Pyrell foam and broadened heating conditions.

testConditions.notes: No oxygen, pressure or airflow setpoints are stated. SAME-R broadened heating temperatures and included no-flow heating periods, per the PSI record, but numeric values are not given.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Quantify low-gravity smoke particle sizes and link size distributions to smoke generation and transport, correcting the TEM-grid contamination problem encountered in SAME.
sensorsAndDiagnostics: DustTrak and ionisation detector (remaining Commercial Diagnostic Enclosure)
Transmission electron microscopy of thermophoretic samples
Post-flight ground tests to validate the lognormal distribution assumption

findings: SAME-R completed 66 test points between 16 July and 9 September 2010.
Three post-flight ground test campaigns were performed to improve data reduction and validate the lognormal distribution assumption used by the moment method.

SAME-R evaluated five spacecraft-relevant materials—Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber, and Pyrell—with low-gravity airflow from quiescent conditions to 8 cm/s and instrument transport times of 11–800 seconds.
Most average smoke-particle sizes were reported in the 200–400 nm range; quiescent cases and longer transport generally produced larger particles. Material-specific morphology differed.

Particle-size distributions were reconstructed from multiple aerosol moments and, for some reported statistics, a log-normal distribution assumption. TEM samples supplied an independent morphology check.
findingsNote: The cited NASA paper describes five materials and the test envelope; values are summary statistics, not a single characteristic size for every material or test.
modelingUtility: Provides a reduced-gravity smoke baseline and validates the lognormal moment-method data reduction used for detector evaluation.
terrestrialApplications: Advanced fire detection for spacecraft and other confined environments (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Detection hardware and smoke-characterisation focus with an unusually concrete operational result (66 test points).

This work supports detector feasibility and operations; it is not a substitute for SAME/SAME-R measurements of smoke generated by heated spacecraft materials.

terrestrialApplications: Adapting aerosol instruments for challenging environments such as submarines or underwater laboratories (PSI record)

fullTitle: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
status: Completed — droplet flammability-limit and suppressant campaign
statusBasis: PSI record gives a closed investigation period and a detailed flight-test procedure.

hardware.facility: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Fluids and Combustion Facility
hardware.apparatus: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) with droplet deployment, fibre support, retractable hot-wire igniter

materials: Other pure and blended liquid fuels in the publications
fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Single droplets, often around 3 mm initial diameter for LOI tests; free or fibre-supported
fuelSpecs.notes: The PSI procedure specifies a smaller droplet size of about 3 mm for the limiting-oxygen-index sequence.

testConditions.notes: PSI gives 0.5–1.5 atm for the LOI tests, converted here to psi (1 atm = 14.6959 psi). Oxygen mole fraction is varied but no overall min/max is stated, so it remains Unknown.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Map flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity, measure gaseous suppressant effectiveness, and determine limiting oxygen index as a function of pressure and suppressant.
variedParameters: Ambient pressure (0.5–1.5 atm for LOI tests)
sensorsAndDiagnostics: Soot and temperature measurements (per PSI objectives)

findings: NASA/TP-2015-216046 documents the apparatus, diagnostics, procedures, analysis methods, and first 284 FLEX tests conducted from March 2009 to December 2011.

The tests used isolated methanol or n-heptane droplets. Reported outputs include initial droplet diameter, visible-flame extinction diameter, droplet burning-rate constant (from a fit of diameter squared versus time), burn time, ambient pressure, and gas composition.

A free-floating droplet and a fiber-supported/moving-droplet method were used in different test configurations; the report explicitly presents data for community analysis rather than a single universal extinction interpretation.
findingsNote: The NASA report is a detailed test record. Individual outcomes depend on fuel, pressure, oxygen and diluent composition, initial droplet size, and test endpoint; consult its test tables instead of generalizing from one run.
modelingUtility: Provides droplet burning-rate and extinction data intended to validate simplified and detailed reduced-gravity combustion models.
terrestrialApplications: Fire suppression in confined environments; cool-flame and low-temperature chemistry relevant to advanced engines (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Suppressant and limiting-oxygen-index focus with a documented pressure range; strong model-validation value. Results are not in the PSI summary.

A NASA-cited FLEX-2 study examined how initial diameter affected convection-free n-heptane, n-octane, and n-decane droplet combustion. The full run-level data and case-specific results should be read from the PSI-68 record and cited publication; the FLEX-1 284-test table is not FLEX-2 data.

terrestrialApplications: Cleaner, more efficient liquid-fuel combustion and surrogate-fuel development (PSI record)

fuelSpecs.notes: BRE is a gas-fueled emulator for condensed fuels, not a solid-fuel test.

namedConditions.label: NASA-considered atmosphere A
namedConditions.note: 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen, as listed in the PSI-20 objectives

namedConditions.label: NASA-considered atmosphere B
namedConditions.note: 10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen, as listed in the PSI-20 objectives

namedConditions.label: NASA-considered atmosphere C
namedConditions.note: 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen, as listed in the PSI-20 objectives

testConditions.notes: These three conditions are described in the PSI record as 'NASA-considered atmosphere for human space missions' that BRE examined. They are experiment test points, not a universal habitat design requirement. O2/CO2 ambients were also desired per the objectives.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Establish quiescent-microgravity burning conditions as functions of material properties, including extinction limits, using gas-fueled porous burners that emulate condensed fuels.
sensorsAndDiagnostics: Burner surface temperature and heat-flux measurements

findings: Quasi-steady burning corresponding to condensed-phase materials such as PMMA and nylon was observed in microgravity without airflow, even though stopping ventilation is an established spacecraft fire-suppression step.

Sustained burning without airflow was notably observed in elevated-oxygen atmospheres being considered for future spacecraft, whereas flames in a 21% oxygen atmosphere self-extinguished in a short time.
The PSI record describes these BRE results as preliminary and suggests greater use of NASA's cone-calorimeter Test 2 for material properties corresponding to the observed microgravity flames.

NASA reports larger flames generally self-extinguished within about 1.5 minutes in the summarized BRE tests; methane flames at elevated oxygen self-extinguished within about a minute, whereas ethylene flames could persist for minutes.
findingsNote: These are preliminary, configuration-specific results summarized by NASA. Larger flames generally self-extinguished within about 1.5 minutes; methane flames at elevated oxygen self-extinguished within about a minute, while ethylene flames could persist for minutes. These results do not constitute operational crew fire-response instructions.
modelingUtility: Provides a flammability map and heat-flux data for modeling quiescent microgravity burning of condensed fuels.
terrestrialApplications: Cone-calorimeter-based material flammability assessment (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Directly tests candidate crew atmospheres and ventilation-loss conditions; strong fire-safety relevance with explicit preliminary caveat.

fullTitle: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame
statusBasis: PSI record gives a closed investigation period; NASA's ACME article describes the six-experiment campaign as completed.

hardware.apparatus: ACME coflow burner with laser extinction, thin-filament pyrometry and chemiluminescence imaging

fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Coflow burner; burner dimensions not stated in the PSI summary
fuelSpecs.notes: Fuels were diluted with nitrogen over a wide range to reach weakly burning and heavily sooting extremes.

testConditions.notes: PSI states that velocity, fuel dilution and soot loading were varied but gives no oxygen, pressure or airflow numbers.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Provide benchmark coflow diffusion-flame data at the extremes of fuel dilution to test computational models, including flame shape, lift-off, temperature, extinction and soot volume fraction.

findings: NASA’s selected ACME findings report 5–8 times more soot in microgravity than in equivalent normal-gravity flames for the compared CLD cases; the microgravity flames were also taller and wider.
The project reported increased fuel-dilution limits for methane and ethylene flames in microgravity; near the limit, some flames were more stable and could remain lifted at lower fuel concentrations.
findingsNote: The 5–8× comparison applies to the cases summarized by NASA, not to all fuels, burner geometries, or microgravity flames.
modelingUtility: Directly targets validation of soot and radiation sub-models for coflow laminar diffusion flames.
terrestrialApplications: Improved soot and radiation models for practical combustors (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Model-validation value is high; direct spacecraft fire-safety relevance is limited for this fundamental flame study.

fullTitle: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
statusBasis: PSI record gives a closed investigation period; NASA's ACME article describes the campaign as completed.

hardware.apparatus: Gas-jet and coflow burners with a high-voltage copper mesh electrode above the burner (up to 10 kV differential)

fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Small focused gas-jet flame and coflow burner configuration

testConditions.notes: PSI states electric field up to 10 kV and varied fuel flow, coflow velocity and polarity, but gives no oxygen or pressure setpoints.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Relate electric-field voltage to chemi-ion current, measure flame response to field changes, evaluate soot formation and characterize near-limit lifted flames.
experimentalDesign.notes: PSI describes the electric field as a flame-control variable, not as a fire-suppression system. No suppression claim is made here.

findings: NASA ACME results report a distinct peak ion current corresponding to the most compact flame in the studied microgravity cases and correlations among flame luminosity, combustion intensity, and ion current.

Weak electric fields stabilized some highly diluted flames. At high field strengths, jet flames became unstable and could develop corona and then arc discharges; soot-bearing flames showed a wider range of responses.
findingsNote: These are research observations, not a spacecraft fire-suppression method validated for operational use.
modelingUtility: Provides ion-current and flame-response data for models of ion-driven convection in electric fields.
terrestrialApplications: Reducing pollutant emissions and improving combustion efficiency with electric fields (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Terrestrial emissions-control focus; PSI explicitly says it was not conducted for space applications. Treated as a surrogate study, not a fire-safety countermeasure.

fullTitle: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
investigationPeriod: PSI record does not list start/end dates
statusBasis: NASA's Combustion Science page lists SPICE among archived experiments. The PSI record has no dates.

hardware.apparatus: Flow duct with integrated nozzles, fuel delivery, cameras and coflow air management

fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Burner diameters 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm and 1.6 mm

testConditions.notes: Coflow velocity range is stated in the PSI approach section. Pressure and oxygen concentration are not stated; tests used coflow air but no numeric O2 value is given.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Identify laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames, and quantify how burner diameter, coflow velocity, fuel and flow rate affect luminous flame length and sooting propensity.
sensorsAndDiagnostics: Still and video cameras for flame length and smoke point
experimentalDesign.notes: PSI reports 526 flames studied across the test matrix; this is a count of tests, not a finding about soot physics.

findings: NASA’s microgravity smoke-point research found steady nonbuoyant jet flames emitted soot more readily than comparable buoyant flames and some earlier short-duration reduced-gravity tests, in part because the long-duration orbit experiment reduced unsteadiness and buoyant motion.

The research measured smoke-point behavior and flame properties over long-duration orbital tests (reported as roughly 100–230 seconds), supporting soot-production models and combustor/fire predictions.
findingsNote: The cited NASA study is a smoke-point investigation. Its results should not be read as an all-fuel ranking or a direct material flammability criterion.
modelingUtility: Provides non-buoyant smoke-point and flame-length data for soot-formation and radiation models.
terrestrialApplications: Soot-formation understanding for cleaner combustion and improved fuel formulation (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Soot and smoke-point science with a large documented matrix; indirect fire-safety relevance.

fullTitle: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames
statusBasis: PSI record classifies the work as a ground investigation with a closed grant period and identifies it as a PSI grant.

hardware.apparatus: Ozone-sensitized counterflow flame experiments and numerical simulations
hardware.notes: The PSI record names 'Principal Investigator Laboratory Hardware' and links a journal article.

fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: Counterflow flame configuration (one-dimensional geometry)

testConditions.notes: The record describes use of FLEX flight conditions and simulations at pressures up to 20 atm, but does not give the ground experiment's oxygen or pressure setpoints. No values are inferred.

experimentalDesign.objectives: Build a flammability-limit diagram for diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion and convection; bridge hot- and cool-flame extinction limits; verify phenomena observed in FLEX.

findings: Warm flames were found to have a double reaction-zone structure and to play a critical role in the transition between cool and hot flames.
In simulations, the flammable region of warm and cool flames expanded with pressure because low- and intermediate-temperature reactivity increases with pressure.
findingsNote: The pressure-expansion result is a simulation finding and should not be described as a measured ISS pressure threshold.
modelingUtility: Tests and extends cool-flame kinetic and radiation models against FLEX data.
terrestrialApplications: Near-limit combustion in high-pressure engines (20–40 atm), engine knock and efficiency (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Uses FLEX flight data to advance cool-flame modeling; limited direct spacecraft hardware relevance.

Stability maps of ignition delay, oscillation and extinction diameters

findings: The PSI summary describes a computational analysis that couples variable-density flow, low-temperature chemical kinetics, and radiation in OpenFOAM, then compares predicted ignition, oscillation, and extinction behavior with ISS FLEX observations.

The intended outputs are stability maps and an explanation for run-to-run differences; the PSI summary does not state a single validated threshold or a complete quantitative map, so none is supplied here.
findingsNote: These statements describe the NASA PSI record’s methods and scope. Simulation-derived conclusions require case-specific comparison with experiment before extrapolation.
modelingUtility: Produces reusable models and sensitivity analyses coupling low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiation.
terrestrialApplications: Engine knock, efficiency and emissions understanding (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Modeling reuse of FLEX data with modest direct spacecraft relevance.

hardware.apparatus: Unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) simulations; two-color tomography of DSLR imagery

fuelSpecs.geometryAndSize: BASS geometries: flat sheets, spheres, rods and wax cylinders

sensorsAndDiagnostics: Flame geometry, temperature, soot volume fraction and spread-rate metrics

findings: BASS/BASS-II supplied experimental benchmarks for time-dependent solid-fuel flame spread and extinction under low-speed forced flow.

NASA’s BASS-II work shows why the near-zero-to-few-cm/s flow regime matters: flames can change rapidly as ventilation changes, so coupled solid heating, gas flow, and flame chemistry are needed to reproduce the observed response.
findingsNote: PSI-62 is a modeling/analysis effort. The statements here describe the experimental phenomena motivating validation, not an independent ISS test result from PSI-62.
modelingUtility: Provides a predictive flammability-limit tool and a potential large-eddy-simulation subgrid model.
terrestrialApplications: Improved combustion and fire-safety modeling on Earth (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Directly reuses BASS flight data to build material-flammability prediction tools for spacecraft.

findings: The SPICE data-reduction work analyzes more than 1,600 DSLR images and derives soot-related quantities and temperature fields from calibrated color imagery.

NASA’s underlying smoke-point research found nonbuoyant, steady flames can emit soot more readily than buoyant flames in the compared cases, so image calibration and consistent diagnostic definitions are essential when comparing gravity environments.

modelingUtility: Improves soot and radiation modeling for both microgravity and terrestrial combustion.
terrestrialApplications: Reducing pollutant emissions and optimizing combustion efficiency (PSI record)

relevanceScores.rationale: Soot-model analysis of existing SPICE data; indirect fire-safety relevance.
